newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Days numbered for Brit backpacker in Hong Kong bar.
newsitem.headline: Days numbered for Brit backpacker in Hong Kong bar.

text.p: The days of the British backpacker hoping to earn a fast buck in Hong Kong are numbered.

Just one week before the last bastion of Britain's oriental empire returns to China, the colony has stripped the immigration privileges of the British who had in the past been able to work here without a visa.
The clock is now ticking away for the army of young hopefuls dubbed "The last of the white coolies" by the Chinese.
Hong Kong had proved an irresistible magnet for the adventurers who stopped off on their round-the-world travels.

They were able at a moment's notice to pick up jobs as waitresses, barmen, construction workers and even shoeshine boys. The fish and chip shops and spit-and-sawdust pubs will no longer echo with London cockney accents.

In the dying days of colonial rule, Hong Kong's legislative council on Monday night overwhelmingly supported the move to bring British passport holders in line with all other foreign nationals living in this capitalist land of opportunity.
The British territory of 6.4 million people returns to Beijing's control at midnight on June 30, putting an end to 156 years of colonial rule.

In April, Britons were stripped of their visa-free residential rights and the council lawmakers have in the last week of their existence given their backing to a new law expected to take effect immediately.
Many backpackers-come-waiters have already sought to extend their lifeline in Hong Kong, once dubbed by novelist Han Suyin "a borrowed place living on borrowed time".
At the end of March, they scurried over to the neighbouring Portuguese enclave of Macao and returned to gain one last 12-month residency stamp before they have to move on.
Accidental tourists abound. Freckle-faced waitress Emily Knapp found Hong Kong to be a real mecca for work.

"I was backpacking in Southeast Asia round Cambodia and Vietnam. I was running out of money and coming to the end of my funds. I got offered three jobs in the same day," she said. Next stop for her is a teaching job in China.
So now bar owners are hunting for local Chinese staff, not an easy task in a city where the average salary is US$25,000. These low-paid jobs offer less than half that.

Roles have ironically been reversed with British travel writer Jan Morris offering a final epitaph to the vanishing breed: "They may not be very skilled workers but by one of Hong Kong's last paradoxes, they charge far less than the Chinese."
